title: Beyond the Chore Chart: What’s Really Driving Falling Fertility?
author: Peter Foreshaw Brookes
summary: Peter Foreshaw Brookes tests Claudia Goldin's "Incomplete Gender Revolution" hypothesis, which says falling birth rates reflect women being left with a double burden of paid work and housework. Using a survey of about 10,000 people in twelve countries from the IFS report Baby Nudges, he and his co-authors find no significant link between feeling overburdened by chores and any fertility indicator, for men or women, parents or childless people, or couples. The one exception was partnered men who felt they did too many chores, who were less likely to intend another child. Objective measures of specific tasks and cross-country comparisons show the same null result. What does predict fertility intentions is values: believing that children are the future of the community, the greatest joy, or important for carrying on the family name. East Asian respondents scored lowest on those beliefs and on religiosity, suggesting cultural differences matter more than chore distribution, though the survey cannot prove causation.
points: The survey found no meaningful relationship between perceived chore burden and intentions to have children.
Even objective measures of household task division showed essentially no link to fertility indicators, both within and across countries.
Beliefs such as "children are the future" explain far more variation in fertility intentions than does chore burden.
Valuing kin and carrying on the family name also predicts wanting more children.
East Asian countries had the lowest levels of those pro-family beliefs and of religiosity, pointing to values rather than household labour.
quotes: Theories about recent declines in fertility have exploded in the past few years, but few have been circulated as widely as that recently popularized by the Nobel Prize-winning economic historian Claudia Goldin: the Incomplete Gender Revolution Hypothesis.

In response, some have suggested that men taking on more housework or child care might help more women to have the children they desire, and others have called for increased government provision or subsidizing of child care.
When we surveyed around 10,000 people across a dozen countries, we failed to find a significant negative association between feeling overburdened by household chores and any fertility indicator.

It appears that, contrary to the hypothesis that women’s burdens reduce fertility, it is within the realm of possibility that men’s fertility intentions may be more sensitive to perceived domestic unfairness. As the chart below shows, all association was driven by male respondents.

There was a weak—and, if anything, positive—cross-country correlation between the share of adults who feel they do more chores than they should and the share who intend to have a(nother) child. Those who value family find themselves intending kids even while doing a lot of work around the house.
In addition, other positive attitudes or beliefs towards family life predict fertility intentions. This applies to the belief that children are the greatest joy.

There is also another striking difference between much of the West and East Asian countries: religious belief. The four East Asian demographics we surveyed (mainland China, Japan, Korea and Chinese speakers overseas in East Asia) all had the lowest religiosity in our international survey, and, accordingly, the lowest rates of the belief that people should have as many children as God gives them.
